authoredPrompt: This figure compares two conformations of ethane, each shown as a Newman projection paired with a ball-and-stick model, with a reaction-style arrow between them. On the left, the Newman projection draws the front carbon as a dot at the center of a circle with three heavy bonds radiating up, down-left, and down-right to hydrogens lettered in green, while the rear carbon is the circle itself with three thinner bonds emerging at the left, right, and bottom to hydrogens lettered in magenta, so the two sets alternate evenly. Its ball-and-stick model, viewed end-on, shows a dark gray carbon ringed by three green and three red spheres in alternating positions. The horizontal arrow between the halves is labeled "Rotate rear carbon 60°". On the right, the projection shows each front bond lying directly over a rear bond, so the green and magenta hydrogens appear in overlapping pairs, and three curly braces, one at each pair, are each labeled "4.0 kJ/mol". The matching model now shows the green and red spheres in coincident pairs. Bold labels read "Ethane—staggered conformation" and "Ethane—eclipsed conformation". Setting the two projections side by side makes the hydrogen spacing the thing being compared, and the three equal energy labels partition the rotational barrier into individual eclipsing interactions.
authoredInteractions:
- Slider for rotating the rear carbon from 0 to 60 degrees; the Newman projection and ball-and-stick model update continuously from staggered to eclipsed, making torsional alignment the source of the conformational change.
- Click for highlighting one eclipsed H-H pair; its brace and 4.0 kJ/mol label brighten along with the overlapping hydrogens, clarifying how three identical interactions add to the rotational barrier.
authoredContext:
Despite what we’ve just said, we actually don’t observe perfectly free rotation in ethane. Experiments show that there is a small (12 kJ/mol; 2.9 kcal/mol) barrier to rotation and that some conformations are more stable than others. The lowest-energy, most stable conformation is the one in which all six C–H bonds are as far away from one another as possible—staggered when viewed end-on in a Newman projection. The highest-energy, least stable conformation is the one in which the six C–H bonds are as close as possible—eclipsed in a Newman projection. At any given instant, about 99% of ethane molecules have an approximately staggered conformation and only about 1% are near the eclipsed conformation.

Staggered conformation of ethane undergoes rotation of rear carbon 60 degrees to form eclipsed conformation of ethane.

The extra 12 kJ/mol of energy present in the eclipsed conformation of ethane is called torsional strain. Its cause has been the subject of controversy, but the major factor is an interaction between C–H bonding orbitals on one carbon and antibonding orbitals on the adjacent carbon, which stabilizes the staggered conformation relative to the eclipsed one. Because a total strain of 12 kJ/mol arises from three equal hydrogen–hydrogen eclipsing interactions, we can assign a value of approximately 4.0 kJ/mol (1.0 kcal/mol) to each single interaction. The barrier to rotation that results can be represented on a graph of potential energy versus degree of rotation, in which the angle between C–H bonds on the front and back carbons as viewed end-on (the dihedral angle) goes full circle from 0 to 360°. Energy minima occur at staggered conformations, and energy maxima occur at eclipsed conformations, as shown in the figure.

discrepancies: Source shows staggered and eclipsed as two separate static panel pairs side by side; generated shows one dynamic pair with a slider (eclipsed state reachable but not visible by default)
Eclipsing-interaction braces are thin arc lines rather than the curly brace annotations in the source
In the ball-and-stick model the rear red hydrogens are fully hidden behind front greens at 60° due to viewing straight down the C–C axis, whereas the source eclipsed model offsets them visibly
Newman projection rear bonds are thinner and lighter than the source's uniformly bold bonds
evaluation.notes: Faithful Newman + ball-and-stick ethane with an excellent torsion slider, energy readout, and clickable eclipsing-pair highlights; only minor annotation styling and eclipsed-view visibility issues.

Render the 4.0 kJ/mol braces as curly-brace shapes to better match the source annotation style
